1.pericope_label: Then the word of the Lord came to Jehu the son of Hanani against Baasha, saying, Forasmuch as I exalted thee out of the dust, and made thee prince over my people Israel; and thou hast walked in the way of Jeroboam, and hast made my people Israel to sin, to provoke me to anger with their sins; Behold, I will take away the posterity of Baasha, and the posterity of his house; and will make thy house like the house of Jeroboam the son of Nebat. Him that dieth of Baasha in the city shall the dogs eat; and him that dieth of his in the fields shall the fowls of the air eat. Now the rest of the acts of Baasha, and what he did, and his might, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel? So Baasha slept with his fathers, and was buried in Tirzah: and Elah his son reigned in his stead. And also by the hand of the prophet Jehu the son of Hanani came the word of the Lord against Baasha, and against his house, even for all the evil that he did in the sight of the Lord, in provoking him to anger with the work of his hands, in being like the house of Jeroboam; and because he killed him.

schools.summary: Henry takes the warning itself for the mercy in it — God threatens that he may not strike, so that repentance might prevent the ruin, or else the ruin appear plainly as justice rather than accident. He sets the prophet beside his father, the elder sent to Judah and the younger on the longer and more dangerous errand north, juniores ad labores, and thinks prophecy so entailed worthy of the more honour. On the exaltation out of the dust he presses that a man who seemed to make himself by treachery was all the while serving a counsel not his own, and that God’s owning the advancement is no patronage of the means. He reads the repeated oracle of Jeroboam’s son and house, and draws the chapter’s sharpest point from it: had Baasha struck with an eye to God’s glory he would have been accepted as a minister of justice, but he was its tool and his own lusts’ servant, which is why those who denounce or execute judgment must do it from a good principle or make themselves obnoxious by it. On the reprieve he will not let a peaceful death pass for escape, since the iniquity is laid up for the children, and he takes the judgment on bodies after death for a tacit intimation of punishments beyond what death can reach.

Gill identifies Jehu as son of the Hanani who reproved Asa, and therefore the son of a prophet then living and himself a young man, since he is found long afterward reproving Jehoshaphat and writing the annals of that reign. He reads the exaltation out of the dust as from a very low estate and a mean family, the removal of the posterity as death leaving no branch remaining, and the dogs and fowls as the denial of burial threatened and executed on the house of Jeroboam before. Baasha’s own death he marks as natural and not violent. On the repeated oracle he reports Abarbinel’s answer, that the first threatening was for making Israel sin and this one for Baasha’s own evil works.

Clarke grants that nothing is known of the prophet beyond this circumstance, and adds that his father Hanani was imprisoned for the faithful discharge of the same ministry to Asa. On the making of a prince he sets a guard against misreading providence: God suffered him to become king in the course of his providence, for it is impossible that God should make a rebel, a traitor and a murderer king over his people, and Scripture habitually represents God as doing what his providence permits. He suspects the seventh verse is out of place and would set it between the fourth and the fifth, and he canvasses four candidates for the man Baasha killed — the Vulgate’s Jehu the prophet, or Baasha, or Jeroboam, or Nadab, the last carrying Jarchi and some good critics with it.

Ellicott makes Jehu probably the son of Hanani the seer of Judah in Asa’s reign, and infers his youth from his rebuking Jehoshaphat after Ahab’s death and writing that reign’s annals. He observes how closely the oracle tracks Ahijah’s against Jeroboam, and draws from the parallel that Baasha had a probation which he neglected, his guilt enhanced by perseverance in the very sins for which vengeance had been inflicted by his own hand. The second reference to the prophecy he takes for a note of the historian, added chiefly for the sake of the last clause, which shows that Baasha’s act, though foretold, was not thereby justified.

Nadab the son of Jeroboam

8.pericope_label: In the twenty and sixth year of Asa king of Judah began Elah the son of Baasha to reign over Israel in Tirzah, two years. And his servant Zimri, captain of half his chariots, conspired against him, as he was in Tirzah, drinking himself drunk in the house of Arza steward of his house in Tirzah. And Zimri went in and smote him, and killed him, in the twenty and seventh year of Asa king of Judah, and reigned in his stead. And it came to pass, when he began to reign, as soon as he sat on his throne, that he slew all the house of Baasha: he left him not one that pisseth against a wall, neither of his kinsfolks, nor of his friends. Thus did Zimri destroy all the house of Baasha, according to the word of the Lord, which he spake against Baasha by Jehu the prophet, For all the sins of Baasha, and the sins of Elah his son, by which they sinned, and by which they made Israel to sin, in provoking the Lord God of Israel to anger with their vanities. Now the rest of the acts of Elah, and all that he did, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel?

schools.summary: Henry measures Elah against the king he replaced in the pattern: Nadab fell in the field of action besieging the same city, where Elah should have been commanding in chief and was not, having loved his ease and safety above his honour, his duty and the public good. From that he draws the drunkard’s warning, that death comes easily on men in that condition, who are the more easily overcome by an enemy and the less able to help themselves, and that it comes terribly, finding them in the act of sin and unfitted for any act of devotion, so that the day arrives unawares. He notes that the traitor succeeded to a people who tamely submitted, that Zimri held by cruelty what he got by treason, that the purge went further than Baasha’s own against Jeroboam’s line in leaving no avengers at all, and that the justice which overtook him so quickly became a proverb long afterward.

Gill counts Elah dead within Asa’s twenty-seventh year, so that the two years are not two full years, and observes that he lasted exactly as long on the throne as Nadab the son of Jeroboam did. Following the Targum he makes Zimri one of two captains over the war-chariots. He has the blow struck while the king was in his drunken fit, and the purge begun perhaps on the very first day of the reign, reaching not only Baasha’s posterity but everyone connected with him even in friendship. The double naming of father and son he reads as proof that Elah trod in Baasha’s steps and was cut off for it.

Keil and Delitzsch extend the suspicion to the host, holding that Arza the prefect of the palace was no doubt a party to the conspiracy and had probably arranged the drinking bout in his own house for the purpose of carrying it out; they gloss the coarse idiom of total destruction as covering males only, explained by the clause that follows it, and render the ground of the destruction closely, that it was on account of all the sins committed through their nothingnesses, by which the golden calves are meant. Ellicott hears in the description of the debauchery an emphasis of half-contemptuous condemnation, since it was public, in the house of a mere officer of the household, and went on while the war was still being fought; he makes Zimri, pointedly called the king’s servant, the high officer left in charge of the palace and the king’s person while the army was in the field, whence his name passed into a proverb for treachery. On the word for those nothingnesses he adds that it covers not only the idols of Dan and Bethel but the worse abominations that grew up under their cover, and that Scripture’s scorn for idolatry as gross folly, faith wasted on unrealities, runs at least as strong as its condemnation of idolatry as outrage against God’s law.

Clarke supposes a colleague not named here who commanded the other half of the cavalry alongside Zimri. On the extermination he reports a rabbinic severity, that when such a sentence is determined not only the man’s own house is destroyed but the five neighbouring houses with it, that his memory may perish from the earth; and he draws from the naming of both father and son the reason judgment was permitted to fall on the family at all, that both were grievous offenders who caused the people to sin and provoked God by their idolatries.

debates.question: How far does the formula of total destruction reach?

positions.view: To males only, the following clause explaining it of avengers and friends
To every kinsman and friend, leaving none at all to avenge him
Further still, to the five neighbouring houses, that the memory may perish from the earth

outliers.claim: Alone in reading a tone of half-contemptuous condemnation into the narrative’s account of the king’s debauchery, noting that it was public and in a subordinate’s house while the war went on.

a king drunk in a servant’s house
the captain of half the chariots

15.pericope_label: In the twenty and seventh year of Asa king of Judah did Zimri reign seven days in Tirzah. And the people were encamped against Gibbethon, which belonged to the Philistines. And the people that were encamped heard say, Zimri hath conspired, and hath also slain the king: wherefore all Israel made Omri, the captain of the host, king over Israel that day in the camp. And Omri went up from Gibbethon, and all Israel with him, and they besieged Tirzah. And it came to pass, when Zimri saw that the city was taken, that he went into the palace of the king’s house, and burnt the king’s house over him with fire, and died, For his sins which he sinned in doing evil in the sight of the Lord, in walking in the way of Jeroboam, and in his sin which he did, to make Israel to sin. Now the rest of the acts of Zimri, and his treason that he wrought, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel? Then were the people of Israel divided into two parts: half of the people followed Tibni the son of Ginath, to make him king; and half followed Omri. But the people that followed Omri prevailed against the people that followed Tibni the son of Ginath: so Tibni died, and Omri reigned.

schools.summary: Henry hears Solomon behind the whole sequence, that for the transgression of a land many are its princes, and notes that the army never avenged Nadab on Baasha, whose house had ruled more gently, but would avenge an idle and intemperate king on his murderer. He calls Tirzah beautiful but unwalled, and reads the self-burning as two motives at once, that a rival should never enjoy the palace and that his own body should not be ignominiously used alive or dead, remarking on the disposition of incendiaries who fire palaces and kingdoms though themselves in danger of perishing in the flame. He supposes Zimri lived some while past the seven days of his proclamation, and in that space showed his inclination and upheld the calves. The division he explains as Zimri’s party joined by those who would not have a king chosen in the camp, lest he rule by the sword and a standing army, but in a convention of the states; he dates the election to Asa’s twenty-seventh year and the unrivalled reign to the thirty-first, and closes with Sir Walter Raleigh’s question why Israel never returned to the house of David, answering with him that dread of a heavier yoke kept them attached to kings of their own.

Gill reads the seven days flatly, that Zimri reigned until the army came up, took the palace and destroyed him. Tidings of the murder came to the host and were displeasing to them. He measures the march from the siege to the royal city at thirty-six miles on Bunting’s reckoning, finds Tirzah lightly fortified and Zimri without force to hold it against such an army, and takes the charge of evil-doing to cover the former part of his life as well as the usurpation. The record of his acts he understands of what he did both before and after the usurpation, and of the manner of the conspiracy. The division he sees as a contested succession, settled very probably by a battle in which Tibni’s party was worsted.

Keil and Delitzsch attach the clause about Zimri’s sins to the verb of dying in the preceding verse, so that he died as a punishment for them; on the division they hold that Omri did not come into undisputed possession at once, that the people of Israel here are probably the fighting people, so that the succession to the throne was decided by the military, and that Omri’s party gained the upper hand after about four years, whereupon Tibni died. Ellicott draws the constitutional moral from how little the elevation needed explaining, that the kingdom of Israel had become entirely the prize of the sword, and notes the coincidence that Baasha’s own dynasty had been founded in the camp before the same city; he judges the conspiracy hastily planned with no adequate means of support, since the capital falls at once. On the word the English renders palace he gives the high place or citadel from its derivation, declining the rendering harem which some adopt and with which the Septuagint’s word for a cave or lurking-place might agree, and he observes that the act has many parallels in Eastern history and suggests something especially treasonable in the assassination of Elah. Of Tibni he knows nothing beyond a probable military rank, perhaps Zimri’s colleague, and reports a brother Joram in the Septuagint who fell with him.

Clarke fills in the campaign: Israel was besieging a Philistine city when word came that Zimri had killed the king, whereupon the troops made their own general king, raised the siege and marched on the royal city, where Zimri, finding his case desperate, chose to consume himself in his palace rather than fall into his enemies’ hands. On the division he confesses that why it took place cannot be told, and distinguishes the sides by institution, the people appearing to be for Tibni and the army for Omri, and the latter prevailing.

23.pericope_label: In the thirty and first year of Asa king of Judah began Omri to reign over Israel, twelve years: six years reigned he in Tirzah. And he bought the hill Samaria of Shemer for two talents of silver, and built on the hill, and called the name of the city which he built, after the name of Shemer, owner of the hill, Samaria. But Omri wrought evil in the eyes of the Lord, and did worse than all that were before him. For he walked in all the way of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, and in his sin wherewith he made Israel to sin, to provoke the Lord God of Israel to anger with their vanities. Now the rest of the acts of Omri which he did, and his might that he shewed, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel? So Omri slept with his fathers, and was buried in Samaria: and Ahab his son reigned in his stead.

schools.summary: Henry makes the building of Samaria the king’s fame, the royal city of Israel ever after now that the palace at Tirzah was burnt, grown in time so considerable that it gave its name to the middle part of the land and to its inhabitants. He reckons the two talents at somewhat more than seven hundred pounds, and offers the conjecture that Shemer may have sold the ground the cheaper on condition the city bear his name, since otherwise it would have borne the purchaser’s. He sets the wandering of Israel’s royal seats — Shechem, then Tirzah, then Samaria — against the constancy of Judah’s kings to Jerusalem, and concludes that those who cleave to the Lord fix while those who leave him ever wander. The infamy he grades above both houses before it, more profane or more superstitious and a greater persecutor, and the aggravation he finds in law: Jeroboam caused Israel to sin by temptation, example and allurement, Omri by compulsion, establishing iniquity by statute. On the might he allows that many a bad man has been a stout man, has built cities and left his name in history, and has no name in the book of life.

Gill reckons the twelve years not from Asa’s thirty-first year but from the twenty-seventh, when Elah was killed, since Ahab began to reign in the thirty-eighth, and reports the division at four years by the Jewish chronology though Jarchi makes it five; the thirty-first is when Omri began to reign over all Israel, at Tibni’s death. He values the talent at three hundred and seventy-five pounds on Brerewood’s reckoning, so that the hill cost seven hundred and fifty. The evil he reads as done openly and publicly, as if in defiance of God, the way of Jeroboam being the worship of the calves, and he marks Omri’s own end as a natural death.

Keil and Delitzsch reckon the twelve years from the rebellion against Zimri, which leaves the sole government only seven years and a few months, from Asa’s thirty-first to his thirty-eighth, and explain the six years at Tirzah as the four of the conflict with Tibni plus two after his death. They value the purchase in thalers, derive the city’s name from the hill’s former owner, note that the Greek keeps one form here and another everywhere else after the Chaldee, and record that Samaria was the royal residence from this time forward and remained the capital of the ten tribes until the kingdom’s destruction. Ellicott reads the accession after the long civil war as opening a new epoch of more settled government and prosperity: the king had to buy peace from Syria by acknowledging its sovereignty and ceding cities, allied himself with the royal house of Tyre both for strength against Syria and for a revival of Solomon’s commerce, and chose his new capital with a soldier’s eye. He takes the name for a watch-tower as well as an owner’s name, describes the isolated hill with its precipitous sides rising in a basin of the hills of Ephraim near the maritime plain and commanding the sea, finds the site vindicated by the long sieges it withstood, and notes that the Assyrian inscriptions call it the house of Omri. The verdict that he did worse than all before him he takes to indicate, besides the development of the old idolatry, some anticipation of the worse idolatry of Baal that Ahab formally introduced, Micah’s statutes of Omri standing in parallel with the works of Ahab’s house as the symbol of hardened apostasy.

Clarke says outright that there must be a mistake in the number thirty-one, since Zimri began to reign in Asa’s twenty-seventh year and Omri immediately succeeded him; he then accepts the harmony he finds in Jarchi out of Sedar Olam, that the division began in the twenty-seventh year and lasted five, during which Omri had but a share of the kingdom, and that at Tibni’s death he held the whole for seven more, the two dates answering to the beginning of the division and to the sole reign. He would render the purchase clause from the Hebrew, that he bought the hill of Shomeron from Shomer and called it Shomeron, Little Shomer, values the two talents at a little over seven hundred pounds, and accounts for the move by Tirzah’s suffering in the civil broils and its burning. He carries the city’s later history through Ben-hadad’s two sieges and Shalmaneser’s three years, Egypt, Antiochus and the Asmoneans, to Herod’s restoration and the name Sebaste. The verdict he grades in four steps, an idolater in principle, in practice, in precept and example, and worst of all in making statutes for idolatry and obliging the people by law to commit it.

29.pericope_label: And in the thirty and eighth year of Asa king of Judah began Ahab the son of Omri to reign over Israel: and Ahab the son of Omri reigned over Israel in Samaria twenty and two years. And Ahab the son of Omri did evil in the sight of the Lord above all that were before him. And it came to pass, as if it had been a light thing for him to walk in the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, that he took to wife Jezebel the daughter of Ethbaal king of the Zidonians, and went and served Baal, and worshipped him. And he reared up an altar for Baal in the house of Baal, which he had built in Samaria. And Ahab made a grove; and Ahab did more to provoke the Lord God of Israel to anger than all the kings of Israel that were before him.

schools.summary: Henry frames the escalation by the commandments: it was nothing to Ahab to break the second by image-worship, so he would set aside the first as well by bringing in other gods, and from that Henry warns that making light of lesser sins makes way for greater and that those who labour to extenuate other men’s sins only aggravate their own. He thinks Ahab knew what his wife would bring and married her for it, describing her as a zealous idolater, imperious and malicious in temper, and judges that this one wife debauched Israel further than all the wives of Solomon. On the god he canvasses three identifications, Jupiter instead of Jehovah, the sun by some accounts, a deified hero of the Phoenicians by others, and adds a motive of his own, that Ahab had grown weary of the golden calves and, like men sick of their own idols, must have variety. He sees rivalry in the siting of the temple, Baal’s house in the royal city because God’s stood in the royal city of the other kingdom, and marvels at idolaters at great expense to befriend one whom they need never have made a god of at all. On the grove he stands alone, arguing from the verb that the text does not say he planted but that he made a grove, something that answered the purpose of concealing and so countenancing the impurities of the worship, since he that doeth evil hateth the light.

Gill marks the difference from the kings before, that they added other idols to the calves and those more abominable, since the earlier kings at least pretended to worship God in the calves whereas Ahab worshipped other gods beside him. The temple at Samaria he explains practically, that the court need not go so far as Tyre or Zidon and that it suited his wife, with an altar reared in it for sacrifice, so open and daring were his idolatrous practices. On the grove he allows a plantation about the temple in which an idol was placed, but prefers to read the word as Astarte herself, the goddess of the Zidonians, an image of which Ahab made.

Keil and Delitzsch put the difference precisely: the kings before Ahab had only perpetuated Jeroboam’s sin, the worship of Jehovah under the image of an ox, and Ahab was not satisfied with that, the Hebrew turning on a question — was it too little? — so that because those sins were too small a thing he took Jezebel, the following verbs being pictorial and marking a new turn of affairs. They identify Ethbaal from Menander in Josephus as king of Tyre and Sidon and priest of Astarte, who usurped the throne after the murder of Pheles, derive Jezebel’s name as probably meaning untouched, and call the grove the Asherah belonging to the temple of Baal, an idol of Astarte. Ellicott identifies the same father-in-law from the same source, notes that he is styled not king of Tyre, as Hiram was, but king of the Zidonians, reviving the older name, and suggests that his priestly origin and that revived spirit may account for the fanatic devotion to Baal visible in Jezebel and in Athaliah, in marked contrast to Hiram’s religious attitude toward Israel. The marriage he reads as the fatal turning-point for a man physically brave and perhaps able as a ruler but morally weak, impressible by good and evil in turn, the history returning again and again to the supremacy of his wife’s relentless nature. The Baal he describes as the Zidonian god worshipped as the productive principle in nature with Astarte as the receptive, insists the name is a title meaning lord, marked as such by the article that almost always precedes it, and therefore applied to the supreme god of various mythologies, surviving in the plural Baalim and in Baal-peor, Baal-berith, Baal-zebub and a string of place-names; the Phoenician Baal was variously represented as the Sun, as the planet Jupiter, and half-humanised as the Tyrian Hercules, and the worship now introduced on a great scale and enforced with a high hand made the conflict with the worship of Jehovah a conflict of life and death.

Clarke locates the head and chief of the offending in the marriage: not merely a heathen but the idolatrous daughter of an idolatrous king, who practised idolatry openly, countenanced and protected it in others and gave its partisans honours and rewards, used every means to persecute the true religion, and put the prophets and priests of God to death with zealous perseverance and relentless cruelty — so that notwithstanding the temple, the altar and the Asherah, his marrying her was esteemed the highest pitch of his vice. On the grove he reads the word as Astarte or Venus, reports that the Syriac calls it an idol and the Arabic a tall tree, and takes the latter for an image of Priapus, the keeper of groves, orchards and gardens.

34.pericope_label: In his days did Hiel the Beth–elite build Jericho: he laid the foundation thereof in Abiram his firstborn, and set up the gates thereof in his youngest son Segub, according to the word of the Lord, which he spake by Joshua the son of Nun.

schools.summary: Henry reads the verse as a subject copying his king’s presumption, and an instance of the height of impiety men had reached, especially at Bethel where one of the calves stood and of which city this daring sinner was. Like Achan he meddled with the accursed thing, turning to his own use what was devoted to God’s honour; he began to build in defiance of a curse well known in Israel, jesting with it perhaps as a bugbear or fancying its force worn out by the five hundred years and more since it was pronounced, and he went on building in defiance of the curse’s partial execution, since though his eldest son died when he began he proceeded in contempt of God and of the wrath revealed from heaven against his ungodliness. He built for his children and God wrote him childless, the eldest dying when he began and the youngest when he finished, with all the rest, it is supposed, between; those whom God curses are cursed indeed, and none ever hardened his heart against God and prospered.

Gill notes that the rebuilding was forbidden by Joshua under an anathema, and allows two possible states of mind in the builder, ignorance of that adjuration or contempt and defiance of it, with the added motive that the work might please the king and queen. Because it was done by Ahab’s leave and under his authority, a private man’s enterprise is mentioned together with the king’s wicked actions.

Keil and Delitzsch read the restoration of a cursed site as a fortification for a measure of how far ungodliness had progressed in Israel, and the fulfilment of the curse upon the builder as showing that the Lord will not allow the word of his servants to be transgressed with impunity; they note that Jericho lay on the border of Ephraim and had been allotted to the Benjaminites, and had come into the possession of the kingdom of Israel when the ten tribes fell away from the royal house. Ellicott reads the same act as marking the growth of prosperity and power as well as the neglect of the old curse, and corrects the assumption that the place had been entirely deserted beforehand; what was new was its importance, which it kept down to the time of Herod. He accounts for that by the ground — well watered and accordingly of great beauty and fruitfulness, the city of palm trees, and of military consequence as commanding the pass from the valley of the Jordan to the high ground of Ai and Bethel — and presses the territorial anomaly hardest: having been assigned to Benjamin it should properly have belonged to the kingdom of Judah, so that its being rebuilt by a Bethelite under Ahab’s patronage is one indication of a half-dependent condition of the southern kingdom at this time.

Clarke will not let the terms of the curse pass as plain, observing that the prediction was delivered upwards of five hundred years before the event and was circumstantially fulfilled, yet the precise meaning of some of its terms is unknown. He sets out three readings of laying the foundation in the firstborn and setting up the gates in the youngest: that the sons died in succession until the family was extinct as the doors were ready to hang; that the words are proverbial for greatly protracted labour, occasioned by multitudinous hindrances, the builder spending on it the whole span in which he was capable of fathering children; or that he sacrificed the firstborn to consecrate the work and the youngest in gratitude at its completion, a reading countenanced by the Chaldee, which has him slay both. He then weighs them: only the Chaldee implies that the children died at all, the Vulgate, Septuagint, Syriac and Arabic do not, and the manuscripts give no help — which strengthens the reading of delays; and he adds two objections, why innocent children should suffer for their father’s presumption, and whether a man who had lost his firstborn at the founding would have gone on at the risk of his whole family. Which opinion is right, or whether any is, he says is more than he can state. He records that the Syriac names Ahab himself as the builder and that the Arabic calls the city a house of idols, and reports a curse still seeming to rest on the place, not blotted from the map but reduced to some thirty wretched cottages and the governor’s dilapidated castle, with no ruin to indicate its former splendour.
